READING

**The two hard deadlines and their sequence**

The Faskally option expires on 2026-12-05 — a fortnight before the Hallowbrand answer is due on 2026-12-19. That gap is notable but does not materially change the analysis; fourteen days of planning progress after validation would tell us almost nothing useful. The decisions are effectively simultaneous.

---

**Dead mileage quantified**

Culverstone sits three miles further from Verrancombe Bridge than Hallowbrand. Each vehicle on the 44 network makes at least one outward and one return dead leg per operating day.

22 vehicles × 6 extra miles × 313 days × £0.63 = **£26,029/year**

That is the permanent annual surcharge from Culverstone, running for the full ten-year term.

Net rent saving of KESTERWICK over ARDENSHAW: £96,000 − £26,029 = **£69,971/year**.

---

**Ten-year financial comparison**

| | ARDENSHAW | KESTERWICK |
|---|---|---|
| Rent × 10 years | £2,140,000 | £1,180,000 |
| Deposit | — | £40,000 |
| Works | — | £480,000 |
| Dead mileage × 10 | — | £260,290 |
| Nethercote (worst case) | — | £64,750 |
| **Total** | **£2,140,000** | **£2,025,040** |

KESTERWICK saves roughly **£115,000 over ten years in the worst planning scenario, £180,000 in the best**. Spread across a decade, that is £11,500–£18,000 a year. That is the full financial prize on offer.

---

**Planning scenarios**

Application validated: 2026-08-14.

| Scenario | Consent | Works complete | Hallowbrand ends | Overlap/gap |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Target (13 wk) | ~2026-11-13 | ~2027-04-10 | 2027-11-30 | 7 months clear |
| Median (34 wk) | ~2027-04-06 | ~2027-10-02 | 2027-11-30 | ~2 months clear |
| Slowest (61 wk) | ~2027-10-16 | ~2028-03-18 | 2027-11-30 | **3½ months on Nethercote** |

The median result gets the fleet off Hallowbrand with weeks rather than months to spare. The worst-ever result puts the company on Nethercote — no workshop, nine miles out — from roughly 1 December 2027 to mid-March 2028. That is the well-described risk in KESTERWICK.

---

**The Nethercote gap is more expensive than it first appears**

£18,500/month × 3.5 months = £64,750 in rent alone. But Nethercote carries no workshop. A fleet of 31 coaches cannot go three to four months without preventive maintenance and unscheduled repair. Buying mobile engineer attendance or sub-contracting to a commercial workshop is an additional and unquantified cost. The operator's licence will also require confirmation of maintenance arrangements. These costs are nowhere in the KESTERWICK arithmetic.

---

**The contract bid is the sharpest exposure**

Bids for the next 44/44A term are due 2027-09-14. Depot cost is a fixed line. The current contract runs to 2028-03-31.

Under ARDENSHAW: the depot cost on the day of signature is £214,000. It goes into the bid exactly.

Under KESTERWICK, the situation at 14 September 2027 depends on planning timing:

- *Best case* (consent Nov 2026, ready April 2027): depot cost is Culverstone at £118,000 plus dead mileage. Fully known.
- *Median case* (ready ~October 2027): the fleet is still at Hallowbrand — whose lease expires seven weeks later. The bid is written with the transition imminent but not complete. Manageable.
- *Worst case* (consent ~October 2027, ready ~March 2028): on bid day the company is running from Nethercote, consent has not yet been granted, and Culverstone will not be ready until after the new contract starts. Do you put Culverstone cost in the bid on the assumption it will be ready for April 2028? If consent then slips further, you have underbid. Do you price Nethercote? That is £222,000/year plus workshop costs — more than ARDENSHAW. Do you bid a blended or hedged figure? Any of these choices introduces error into the most important commercial submission of the next two years, for a contract whose margin is already constrained by the tender process.

Worst-case KESTERWICK and the 2027-09-14 bid is a collision of two material uncertainties at the worst possible moment. ARDENSHAW eliminates that collision entirely.

---

**Planning refusal**

No refusal rate is given, but the risk is real and the outcome is not merely inconvenient. If consent is refused outright:

- The £40,000 deposit is gone.
- The Hallowbrand offer has lapsed.
- Culverstone is an option on a site that cannot be used as a depot without consent.
- An appeal could run six months or more; the site option expires 2028-06-30.
- The company needs 31-vehicle accommodation from 2027-11-30 without a workshop and without any negotiating position with the Hallowbrand landlord.

The landlord, knowing the company has nowhere else to go, would not be constrained to the terms offered in 2026. This scenario is not the probable outcome; it is the tail event that the cash buffer and the £200,000 facility are wholly insufficient to price.

---

**Cash and liquidity**

Available today: £640,000 cash plus £200,000 facility.

KESTERWICK would require £40,000 in December and £480,000 once consent is granted. In the best-case scenario the works begin within three months of now; the company pays out £520,000 and is left with roughly £120,000 cash before the facility. Continuing obligations — fleet insurance, wages, fuel, VAT — run against that balance. It is serviceable but leaves no cushion for an adverse operational event.

ARDENSHAW requires no capital and preserves the full £840,000 of headroom throughout. That resilience has operational value independent of the depot decision.

---

**Paybck on the capital**

At £69,971 net annual saving, the £520,000 capital of KESTERWICK is repaid in approximately 7.4 years — deep into the ten-year term. The benefit accrues almost entirely in years eight to ten. The lease at Culverstone, like Hallowbrand, is a tenancy; the £480,000 in works goes with the building at term end. There is no residual asset. The case that the investment is "money we get back" holds — just barely within the term — but it holds only if planning runs to the median or better, and only if no planning costs beyond the application fee are incurred, and only if Nethercote workshop costs are zero. Strip out the optimistic assumptions and the margin disappears.

---

**Balancing the case**

KESTERWICK is cheaper in every planning scenario when measured only against rent and known capital. The difficulty is that the financial advantage is narrow and back-loaded, while the risks — planning refusal, Nethercote without a workshop, and the bid submission under uncertainty — are front-loaded and concentrated in the period that matters most to the company's primary revenue.

The £11,500–£18,000 average annual saving does not adequately compensate for carrying unquantified planning risk on a business whose licence, contract, and staff depend on uninterrupted depot function. ARDENSHAW is not cheap; a 52 per cent rent increase over the current passing rate is a real cost. But it converts every uncertain variable into a single known number before the month is out.

READING

CALL
ARDENSHAW

GROUNDS
The net ten-year saving from KESTERWICK averages below £18,000 a year, and that saving is back-loaded into years eight to ten, while the planning refusal risk, the workshop-less Nethercote exposure, and the danger of entering the September 2027 contract bid without a settled depot cost are all front-loaded into the period on which the 44 and 44A franchise depends.
